newsitem.title: CHINA: HK said planning rush law to oust hundreds of kids.
newsitem.headline: HK said planning rush law to oust hundreds of kids.

text.p: The Hong Kong government will ask law-makers next Wednesday to empower an immediate repatriation of hundreds of illegal child migrants from the Chinese mainland, a newspaper said on Saturday.

The Chinese-language Hong Kong Economic Times said the post-colonial government would ask the China-appointed interim assembly to rush through the law so the government could expel young Chinese illegals here without proof of identity.
Hong Kong police chief Eddie Hui vowed on Saturday to stop illegal migrants trying to sneak into the former British colony at the border.
He spoke to reporters before leaving for talks with Chinese officials on the issue in the frontier city of Shenzhen.
"We will make sure the illegals do not pass through the border," Hui said.
Shenzhen, bordering with Hong Kong, is where most illegals come from, lured by visions of a better life in the region.
On Friday, hundreds of families flocked to Hong Kong's immigration headquarters to surrender illegal immigrant children who had sneaked in from China, hoping they would be allowed to stay.
The rush was sparked by an announcement on Thursday that "child illegals" could remain here while their parents' background was checked to determine if they had a right to stay.
The office of Hong Kong's leader Tung Chee-hwa was not immediately available for comment.

Hong Kong's new constitution, the Basic Law, which took effect on Tuesday when the former British colony became a quasi-autonomous Chinese territory, says mainland-born offspring of a Hong Kong permanent resident are entitled to stay here.

But under current arrangements, they must apply to Chinese authorities for permission to migrate to Hong Kong, which can mean a wait for years as only 150 Chinese immigrants, about 66 of them children, are allowed into the territory each day.
It is estimated that 60,000 children from "separate families" are waiting to settle in the territory.
Although Hong Kong reverted to China earlier this week, border control between the two place remains intact.
